name: Custom layout
first: A type of your own that sizes and places the views inside it by a rule that SwiftUI's own containers do not have.

dependsOn.why: A custom layout is the parent in the steps of layout: it chooses its own size, and proposes a size to each view and places it.
dependsOn.whyInExample: `place(at:proposal:)` proposes `step`, 30 by 30, to each color, as each renderer proposes a size on the page of Layout process.

dependsOn.why: A custom layout is a type that conforms to SwiftUI's layout protocol.
dependsOn.whyInExample: `Stairs` conforms to the protocol `Layout`, and has the two methods that it requires.

what.is: A custom layout is a type that conforms to the protocol `Layout`. It is the parent in the steps of layout: its method `sizeThatFits` chooses its size, and its method `placeSubviews` places each view inside it, with a proposal for that view's size. Used with braces, as on line 28, it lays out the views listed in them.
what.afterExample: `Stairs` makes each view 30 by 30 points, and places each one 30 points further right and further down than the one before. Three views make stairs of 90 by 90.
what.problem: Stacks and grids cover most layouts, but not every one, such as a row of chips that wraps onto the next line, or views in a circle. A custom layout writes that rule once, and any views can use it.
what.how: SwiftUI calls `sizeThatFits` with the proposal from the layout's parent, and with the views inside it, as `subviews`, and uses the size it returns. Then it calls `placeSubviews` with `bounds`, the space that the layout got, and the layout calls `place(at:proposal:)` on each view, which gives the view a proposal and a place.

when.text: Use one for a rule of placement that stacks and grids cannot express, such as a row that wraps, or stairs.
Don't use one when a stack or a grid does the job: they are already written, and they handle spacing and alignment for you.

parts.name: The conformance to `Layout`, line 3
parts.text: The colon and the name `Layout` after `Stairs` say that `Stairs` conforms to the protocol `Layout`, which requires two methods, `sizeThatFits` and `placeSubviews`. Their last parameter, `cache`, can keep values between calls. `Stairs` keeps none, so the type of `cache` is `inout ()`, an empty value.

parts.name: The method `sizeThatFits`, lines 4 to 11
parts.text: The method `sizeThatFits` returns the size that the layout chooses. It gets the proposal from its parent, and `subviews`, the views inside the layout. Line 9 multiplies 30 by the number of views, and line 10 returns a square of that side, whatever the proposal.

parts.name: The method `placeSubviews`, lines 12 to 24
parts.text: The method `placeSubviews` gets `bounds`, the space that the layout got, and places each view in it. Line 18 starts at the top leading corner of `bounds`. For each view, line 20 calls `place(at:proposal:)`, which puts the view at `corner` and proposes it `step`, 30 by 30, from line 27. Lines 21 and 22 move `corner` 30 points right and 30 points down.

steps.text: Line 27 makes `step`, a proposal of 30 by 30, and line 28 makes a `Stairs` that lays out the three colors listed in its braces.
Line 33 makes a renderer, and line 34 asks for the image, so SwiftUI lays out `stairs`.
SwiftUI calls `sizeThatFits`. There are 3 views, so line 9 works out 90, and line 10 chooses 90 by 90.
SwiftUI calls `placeSubviews`. Line 20 places the blue color at the top leading corner, proposed `step`, the green one 30 points right and down from it, and the red one 60 points right and down.
Line 35 prints the size of the image, which is the size that `Stairs` chose: {{90 90}}.

end.text: `Stairs` chose its own size from the number of its views, and placed each one by its own rule, one step down and to the right.
